conservation.condition_narrative:
The work appears to be unlined and is lightly varnished; a label on the verso indicates it was sprayed with Lucite 46 by Felrath Hines in 1967. This varnish imparts an even, moderate sheen overall. The painting is in very good condition with few losses; stretcher bar cracks are developing along the right, top and left sides. 
The painting is housed in a thin profile, round-face, painted wooden frame that may be original. The frame was either repainted or has yellowed considerably. While it is currently a warm yellow-beige, residues on the verso suggest it was originally white. The painting is held into this frame by nails, retains O'Keeffe's original cardboard backing, and has not been removed since before its acquisition in 2002.
conservation.report_notes: Information provided for *Access O'Keeffe* by Art Institute of Chicago in 2025.
conservation.technical_description: The painting is executed on canvas with a white ground mounted to a four-member keyable stretcher. The work is relatively thinly painted in a limited number of wet-in-wet campaigns. The ground color plays a crucial role in the composition, left visible in some areas near the edges of forms such as the lower left corner of the house. While much of the paint layer is opaque, O'Keeffe employed translucent yellow-greens throughout the foreground. The foreground pushes forward in space, appearing to almost glow as the bright ground shows through. O'Keeffe employed relatively flat-tipped, stiff-bristle brushes so that the surface retains evidence of its working. The short, parallel hatches in the foreground grass contrast with an almost stippled handling in the trees and sky; here, the bristles curled against the surface from the pressure of the artist's hand.

cr_data.provenance: Georgia O’Keeffe (1887–1986), New York and New Mexico, then Abiquiú, NM, from 1949; sold to Paul Rosenbaum (1897–1982) and Gabriella Rosenbaum (1905–2000; born Gabriella Kramer), Chicago and Palm Springs, FL, 1967 [documentation in curatorial object file]; by descent to Gabriella Rosenbaum; bequeathed to the Art Institute of Chicago, 2002. (Source: Art Institute of Chicago, 2025)
remarks_1999: Double entries Whitney Archive, Downtown Gallery Archive. Entries in Whitney Archive and Abiquiú Notebooks indicate, "Exam. at Amer. Place, April 1946... [note of backing inscription 2]. This is the little house with flagpole. It is not the 1925 one of which I have a photograph and I don't think the same as the one in the gallery photograph. I doubt also whether it is the same as the 1924 'Flagpole' of which I have a photograph, but as I did not compare at the time and have to rely on memory I am not quite sure about it." Abiquiú Notebooks indicates backing inscription 3. Whitney Archive indicates, "Painted 1924." Whitney Archive, Downtown Gallery Archive date 1923 and 1924. Abiquiú Notebooks dates 1923. Either this or cat. no. 361 or 481 mentioned in 1934 New York (An American Place) exhibition review in *New York Times* (1934). Reproduced and titled *The Flagpole (First Painting)* in *The Dial* (May 1925). See cat. nos. 361, 481. (Source: Lynes, 1999)

credit_line: Bequest of Paul and Gabriella Rosenbaum, 2002.72
description: Exuberantly flowering yellow green and purple trees stand against a bright blue sky dotted with a few white clouds. In front of the trees is a white house with a gray pitched roof. A black doorway with a green awning disrupts the smooth white surface of the house. In the foreground is a low grassy mound with a tall white pole extending past the edge of the canvas.
